{{Modern physics}}

'''Yang Chen-Ning''' ({{lang-zh|t=楊振寧|s=杨振宁|p=Yáng Zhènníng}}; October 1, 1922 – October 18, 2025) also known as '''C.N. Yang''' and '''Franklin Yang''',<ref name="npbio">{{Cite web |title=Chen Ning Yang – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1957/yang/biographical/ |publisher=The Nobel Foundation |access-date=November 27, 2020 |archive-date=February 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210215153/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1957/yang/biographical/ |url-status=live }}</ref> was a Chinese-American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] who made significant contributions to [[statistical mechanics]], [[integrable systems]], [[gauge theory]], [[particle physics]] and [[condensed matter physics]].

Yang is known for his collaboration with [[Robert Mills (physicist)|Robert Mills]] in 1954 in developing non-abelian gauge theory, widely known as the [[Yang–Mills theory]], which describes the [[nuclear force]]s in the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics.

Yang and [[Tsung-Dao Lee]] received the 1957 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]]<ref name="np">{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1957 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1957/summary/ |publisher=The Nobel Foundation |access-date=October 18, 2025 |archive-date=May 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200522211742/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1957/summary/ |url-status=live }}</ref> for their work on parity non-conservation of the [[weak interaction]], which was confirmed by the [[Wu experiment]] in 1956. The two proposed that the conservation of [[parity (physics)|parity]], a physical law observed to hold in all other physical processes, is violated in weak nuclear reactions – those nuclear processes that result in the emission of [[beta particle]]s.

== Early life and education ==
Yang was born in [[Hefei]], Anhui, China, on October 1, 1922.<ref name="birthdate">{{Cite web |last1=Li |first1=Bing-An |last2=Deng |first2=Yuefan |author-link2=Yuefan Deng |title=Biography of C.N. Yang |url=http://insti.physics.sunysb.edu/~yang/yangbio.pdf |access-date=September 11, 2007 |quote=His birth date was erroneously recorded as September 22, 1922 in his 1945 passport. He has since used this incorrect date on all subsequent official documents. |archive-date=January 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210107183053/http://insti.physics.sunysb.edu/~yang/yangbio.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> His mother was Luo Meng-hua and his father, {{ill|Yang Ko-Chuen|lt=Ko-Chuen Yang|zh|杨武之}} ({{lang|zh-Hant|楊克純}}; 1896–1973), was a mathematician.<ref name="birthdate" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Close |first=Frank |date=October 21, 2025 |title=Chen-Ning Yang obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2025/oct/21/chen-ning-yang-obituary |access-date=October 22, 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite Q|Q138460112}}</ref>

Yang attended elementary school and high school in [[Beiping]] (now [[Beijing]]), and in the autumn of 1937 his family moved to Hefei after the [[Second Sino-Japanese War#1937: Full-scale invasion of China|Japanese invaded China]].<ref name="nytimes obit">{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=George |date=October 18, 2025 |title=Chen Ning Yang, Nobel-Winning Physicist, Is Dead at 103 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/18/science/chen-ning-yang-dead.html |accessdate=October 18, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> In 1938 they moved to [[Kunming]],<ref name="nytimes obit" /> Yunnan, where [[National Southwestern Associated University]] was located. In the same year, as a second-year student, Yang passed the entrance examination and studied at National Southwestern Associated University. He received a Bachelor of Science in 1942,<ref name="npbio" /> with his thesis on the application of [[group theory]] to molecular spectra, under the supervision of [[Wu Ta-You|Ta-You Wu]].<ref name="birthdate" />

Yang continued to study graduate courses there for two years under the supervision of [[Wang Zhuxi]] (J.S. Wang), working on statistical mechanics. In 1944, he received a Master of Science from [[National Tsing Hua University]], which had moved to Kunming during the Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945).<ref name="npbio" /> Yang was then awarded a scholarship from the [[Boxer Indemnity Scholarship Program]], set up by the United States government using part of the money China had been forced to pay following the [[Boxer Rebellion]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Lautz |first=Terry |chapter=Chen-ning Yang: Science and Patriotism |date=March 3, 2022 |title=Americans in China |pages=90–111 |chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/book/38931/chapter/338112301 |access-date=October 20, 2025 |edition=1 |publisher=Oxford University PressNew York |language=en |doi=10.1093/oso/9780197512838.003.0005 |isbn=978-0-19-751283-8|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> His departure for the United States was delayed for one year, during which time he taught in a middle school as a teacher and studied field theory.<ref name="birthdate" />

Yang entered the [[University of Chicago]] in January 1946 and studied with [[Edward Teller]].<ref name=":9" /> He received a Doctor of Philosophy in 1948.<ref name="npbio" />

== Career ==
Yang remained at the [[University of Chicago]] for a year as an assistant to [[Enrico Fermi]].<ref name="nytimes obit" /> In 1949 he was invited to do his research at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]], New Jersey, where he began a period of fruitful collaboration with [[Tsung-Dao Lee]].<ref name="nytimes obit" /> Lee and Yang published 32 papers together.<ref name="nytimes obit" /> He was made a permanent member of the Institute in 1952, and full professor in 1955. In 1963, [[Princeton University Press]] published his textbook, ''Elementary Particles''. In 1965 he moved to [[Stony Brook University]], where he was named the Albert Einstein Professor of Physics and the first director of the newly founded Institute for Theoretical Physics. Today this institute is known as the [[C. N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics]].<ref name="npbio" /> Yang retired from Stony Brook University in 1999.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 18, 2010 |title=Exclusive: New Dorm Likely to Honor Nobel Laureate |url=http://thinksb.com/2010/03/exclusive-new-dorm-likely-to-honor-nobel-laureate/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717045917/http://thinksb.com/2010/03/exclusive-new-dorm-likely-to-honor-nobel-laureate/ |archive-date=July 17, 2011 |access-date=May 6, 2011 |website=Thinksb.com}}</ref>

Yang visited mainland China in 1971 for the first time after the thaw in China–US relations, and subsequently worked to help the Chinese physics community rebuild the research atmosphere,<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Sadovskii |first=Michael V. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J5adDwAAQBAJ&dq=yang+1971+for+the+first+time+after+the+thaw+in+China%E2%80%93US+relations,+and+has+subsequently+worked+to+help+the+Chinese+physics+community+rebuild+the+research+atmosphere&pg=PT62 |title=Quantum Field Theory |date=May 20, 2019 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG |isbn=978-3-11-064526-2 |language=en}}</ref> which later eroded due to political movements during the [[Cultural Revolution]].<ref name=":1" /> After retiring from Stony Brook, he returned to Beijing as an honorary director of [[Tsinghua University]],<ref name=":1" /> where he was the first Huang Jibei-Lu Kaiqun Professor at the [[Center for Advanced Study, Tsinghua University|Center for Advanced Study]] (CASTU).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Huang Changfeng Donates 3.6 Million USD to Center for Advanced Study |url=https://www.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/info/1245/3457.htm |access-date=October 18, 2025 |website=Tsinghua University }}</ref> He was also one of the two [[Shaw Prize]] Founding Members and was a Distinguished Professor-at-Large at the [[Chinese University of Hong Kong]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 18, 2025 |title=Chinese Nobel Prize-winning physicist Chen Ning Yang dies at 103 |url=https://abcnews.go.com/International/wireStory/chinese-nobel-prize-winning-physicist-chen-ning-yang-126640875 |access-date=October 18, 2025 |website=ABC News |language=en |archive-date=October 18, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251018190831/https://abcnews.go.com/International/wireStory/chinese-nobel-prize-winning-physicist-chen-ning-yang-126640875 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Yang helped to establish the Theoretical Physics Division at the [[Chern Institute of Mathematics]] in 1986 at the request of [[Shiing-Shen Chern]] who was serving as the inaugural director of the Institute at the time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introduction-CIM |url=http://en.cim.nankai.edu.cn/About_CIM/Introduction.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250219222902/http://en.cim.nankai.edu.cn/About_CIM/Introduction.htm |archive-date=February 19, 2025 |access-date=February 19, 2025 |website=en.cim.nankai.edu.cn}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Theoretical Physics Division-CIM |url=http://en.cim.nankai.edu.cn/Affiliations/Theoretical_Physics_Division.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250219231743/http://en.cim.nankai.edu.cn/Affiliations/Theoretical_Physics_Division.htm |archive-date=February 19, 2025 |access-date=February 19, 2025 |website=en.cim.nankai.edu.cn}}</ref>

== Personal life and death ==
Yang married Tu Chih-li ({{lang-zh|first=t|t=杜致禮|s=杜致礼|p=Dù Zhìlǐ}}), a teacher, in 1950; they had two sons and a daughter together. His father-in-law was the [[Kuomintang]] general [[Du Yuming]]. Tu died in October 2003. In January 2005, Yang married Weng Fan ({{lang-zh |t = 翁帆 |p = Wēng Fān }}), a university student. They met in 1995 at a physics seminar; the couple reestablished contact in February 2004 when Yang moved to China to become affiliated with [[Tsinghua University]]. Yang called Weng, who was 54 years his junior, his "final blessing from God".<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 16, 2014 |title=Chen Ning Yang, 82, to marry a 28-year-old woman |url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/english/doc/2004-12/16/content_400791.htm |work=[[China Daily]] |archive-date=March 1, 2017 |access-date=January 29, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301054217/http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/english/doc/2004-12/16/content_400791.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

Yang obtained U.S. citizenship during his research within the country. According to the state-run Xinhua News Agency, Yang said the decision was painful as his father never forgave him for that. According to Xinhua and other mainstream Chinese media, he formally renounced his American citizenship on April 1, 2015. He acknowledged that while the U.S. was a beautiful country that gave him good opportunities to study science, China since his youth had offered the best secondary and undergraduate institutions, though the US had the top graduate studies. However, circumstances changed in favor of China's growth by the turn of the century.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Yang Zhenning Courts Controversy|url=https://u.osu.edu/mclc/2017/02/25/yang-zhenning-courts-controversy/}}</ref><ref>{{YouTube|6d3hZ8jnqXg|C. N. Yang: Stony Brook Masters Series}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=February 24, 2017 |title=Two top Chinese-American scientists have dropped their U.S. citizenship |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/two-top-chinese-american-scientists-have-dropped-their-us-citizenship |work=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |archive-date=December 19, 2022 |access-date=December 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221219191552/https://www.science.org/content/article/two-top-chinese-american-scientists-have-dropped-their-us-citizenship |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url = https://apnews.com/article/china-nobel-laureate-physicist-chen-ning-yang-fb5709847c4dbe01e967e5eb1df28c18 | title = Chinese Nobel Prize-winning physicist Chen Ning Yang dies at 103 | date = October 18, 2025 | accessdate = October 18, 2025 | work = [[Associated Press News]] }}</ref>

His son Guangnuo was a computer scientist.<ref>[https://www.laitimes.com/en/article/398to_3py6a.html LA Times, 2022-03-01]</ref> His second son Guangyu is an astronomer, and his daughter Youli is a doctor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Important Events in the Life of Chen Ning Yang (CNY) |url=https://www.ias.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/Events2022.pdf}}</ref>

Yang [[centenarian|turned 100]] on October 1, 2022,<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 21, 2022 |title=Celebrating Chen Ning Yang at 100 |url=https://www.ias.edu/news/celebrating-chen-ning-yang-100 |access-date=September 30, 2022 |website=Institute for Advanced Study |language=en |archive-date=June 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603133923/https://www.ias.edu/news/celebrating-chen-ning-yang-100 |url-status=live }}</ref> and died in Beijing on October 18, 2025, at the age of 103.<ref name="dies">{{cite news |last1=Chen |first1=Stephen |last2=Xin |first2=Ling |date=October 18, 2025 |title=Chinese Nobel Prize-winning physicist Chen-ning Yang dies, aged 103 |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3329496/chinese-nobel-prize-winning-physicist-chen-ning-yang-dies-aged-103 |access-date=October 18, 2025 |newspaper=[[South China Morning Post]] |archive-date=October 18, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251018070856/https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3329496/chinese-nobel-prize-winning-physicist-chen-ning-yang-dies-aged-103 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="nytimes obit" /> The day after the announcement of his death, people gathered and waited in line at Tsinghua University to pay tributes to Yang.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zou|first=Shuo |title=Scientific community, netizens pay tribute to late Nobel laureate Yang Chen-Ning |url=https://global.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202510/19/WS68f4f914a310f735438b5cd1.html |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=global.chinadaily.com.cn}}</ref>

== Views on the CEPC ==
Yang is known for having opposed the construction of the [[Circular Electron Positron Collider]] (CEPC), a 100&nbsp;km circumference particle collider in China that would study the [[Higgs boson]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Banks |first=Michael |date=October 21, 2025 |title=Influential theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate Chen-Ning Yang dies aged 103 |url=https://physicsworld.com/influential-theoretical-physicist-and-nobel-laureate-chen-ning-yang-dies-aged-103/ |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> He catalogued the project as "guess" work and without guaranteed results. Yang said that "even if they see something with the machine, it's not going to benefit the life of Chinese people any sooner."<ref name=":7" />

== Academic achievements ==
Yang worked on [[statistical mechanics]], [[condensed matter theory]], [[particle physics]] and [[gauge theory]]/[[quantum field theory]].

Various Nobel Prizes in Physics are based on Yang's work. At least 10 Nobel laureates in Physics cited Yang's work during their Nobel speech, this includes: [[Steven Weinberg]] (1979), [[Sheldon Glashow]] (1979), [[Martinus J. G. Veltman]] (1999), [[Gerard 't Hooft]] (1999), [[David Gross]] (1999), [[Yoichiro Nambu]] (2008), [[Makoto Kobayashi]] (2008), [[Toshihide Maskawa]] (2008), [[François Englert]] (2013) and [[Peter Higgs]] (2013).<ref name=":4" />

=== Early contributions ===
His first two papers (1944, 1945) were the result of his master thesis on statistical physics, supervised by [[Wang Zhuxi|J. S. Wang]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fisher |first=Michael E. |date=December 10, 2015 |title=Statistical physics in the oeuvre of Chen Ning Yang |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0217979215300133 |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics B |volume=29 |issue=30 |pages=1530013 |doi=10.1142/S0217979215300133 |bibcode=2015IJMPB..2930013F |issn=0217-9792|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

At the University of Chicago, Yang first spent twenty months working in an accelerator lab, but found he was not good at [[experimental physics]] and switched back to theory. His doctoral thesis was about an atomic beam apparatus for measuring the [[nuclear quadrupole resonance]] of sodium.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Ge |first1=Mo-lin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kkHICgAAQBAJ&dq=cn+yang+doctoral+thesis+nuclear&pg=PA14 |title=Proceedings of the Conference in Honor of C. N. Yang's 85th Birthday: Statistical Physics, High Energy, Condensed Matter and Mathematical Physics |last2=Oh |first2=Choo Hiap |last3=Phua |first3=Kok Khoo |date=December 12, 2008 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4471-56-5 |language=en}}</ref>

Later, Yang worked on particle phenomenology; a well-known work was the Fermi–Yang model of 1949, treating the [[pion]] as a bound nucleon–antinucleon pair.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sitenko |first1=A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e6XqCAAAQBAJ&dq=Fermi%E2%80%93Yang+model&pg=PA516 |title=Theory of Nucleus: Nuclear Structure and Nuclear Interaction |last2=Tartakovskii |first2=V. |date=December 6, 2012 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-011-5772-8 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Main contributions ===
[[File:Yang.jpg|thumb|upright|Yang in 1957]]

Yang is well known for his 1953 collaboration with [[Robert Mills (physicist)|Robert Mills]] in developing [[Non-abelian group|non-abelian]] [[gauge theory]], widely known as the [[Yang–Mills theory]].<ref name=":2" /> The idea was generally conceived by Yang while the novice scientist Mills assisted him as Mills explained:<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gray |first1=Jeremy |author-link1=Jeremy Gray (mathematician) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e0TTBwAAQBAJ&q=during+the+academic+year+1953-1954+yang+was+a+visitor+to+the+brookhaven+national+laboratory...+I+was+at+brookhaven+also...+and+was+assigned&pg=PA63 |title=Mathematical Conversations: Selections from The Mathematical Intelligencer |last2=Wilson |first2=Robin |author-link2=Robin Wilson (mathematician) |date=December 6, 2012 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=9781461301950 |page=63}}</ref><blockquote>During the academic year 1953–54, Yang was a visitor to [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]&nbsp;... I was at Brookhaven also&nbsp;... and was assigned to the same office as Yang. Yang, who demonstrated on a number of occasions his generosity to physicists beginning their careers, told me about his idea of generalizing gauge invariance and we discussed it at some length&nbsp;... I was able to contribute something to the discussions, especially with regard to the quantization procedures, and to a small degree in working out the formalism; however, the key ideas were Yang's.</blockquote>

[[The Scientist (magazine)|''The Scientist'']] called Yang–Mills theory:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ravo |first=Nick |date=October 2, 1999 |title=Robert L. Mills, 72, Theorist In Realm of Subatomic Physics |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/10/30/nyregion/robert-l-mills-72-theorist-in-realm-of-subatomic-physics.html |website=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=March 29, 2021 |archive-date=November 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231105155019/https://www.nytimes.com/1999/10/30/nyregion/robert-l-mills-72-theorist-in-realm-of-subatomic-physics.html |url-status=live }}</ref><blockquote>
The foundation for the current understanding of how subatomic particles interact is a contribution which has restructured modern physics and mathematics.</blockquote>In 1956, he and T. D. Lee analyzed a problem known as the τ–θ puzzle, in which a particle called θ decayed into two [[pion]]s and a particle τ into three pions, the two decays with different [[Parity (physics)|parity symmetry]].<ref name=":8" /> However the two particles were not distinguishable.<ref name=":8" /> Lee and Yang proposed that, in the [[weak interaction]], [[parity symmetry]] was not conserved and that it was the same particle (now known as the [[kaon]] K<sup>+</sup>).<ref name=":8" /> To test if weak interaction conserved parity, Lee contacted [[Chien-Shiung Wu]]'s team at the National Bureau of Standards in Washington. [[Wu experiment]] experimentally verified the theory and the results were announced early in a press conference.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2012 |title=Credit where credit's due? |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/credit-where-credits-due/ |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB |archive-date=September 17, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250917121036/https://physicsworld.com/a/credit-where-credits-due/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The results were also confirmed by two other independent experiments by [[Valentine Telegdi]] and [[Jerome Isaac Friedman]] at the [[University of Chicago]] and by [[Richard Garwin]] and [[Leon M. Lederman]] at [[Columbia University]].<ref name=":8" /> All three experiments published their results in early 1957.<ref name=":8" /> That year, Yang and Lee received the 1957 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] for this parity violation theory, which brought revolutionary change to the field of particle physics.<ref name="np" />

In the 1970s, Yang worked on the topological properties of gauge theory, collaborating with [[Tai Tsun Wu]] to elucidate the [[Wu–Yang monopole]], a type of [[magnetic monopole]]. Unlike the [[Dirac monopole]], it has no singular [[Dirac string]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ortín |first=Tomás |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HDmucsxABzYC&dq=wu+yang+monopole&pg=PA254 |title=Gravity and Strings |date=2004 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-03546-0 |language=en}}</ref> Their 1975 paper, known as the [[Wu–Yang dictionary]], helped bridge gaps between physics and differential geometry.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 1, 2015 |title=Historical note on fiber bundles |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/letters/historical-note-on-fiber-bundles |access-date=October 18, 2025 |website=PHYSICS TODAY |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Ji |first1=Lizhen |author-link=Lizhen Ji |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o4xBEQAAQBAJ&dq=wu+yang+dictionary+physics&pg=PA76 |title=Living Record Of Scientific History, The: Conversations With C N Yang |last2=Wang |first2=Liping |date=December 27, 2024 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-12-8495-3 |language=en}}</ref>

On Yang's retirement from SUNY in 1999, [[Freeman Dyson]] called Yang "the pre-eminent stylist" of 20th-century physics alongside [[Albert Einstein]] and [[Paul Dirac]], citing how Yang "turns his least important calculations into miniature works of art, and turns his deeper speculations into masterpieces."<ref name="nytimes obit" /> In 2009, Dyson wrote:<ref name=":4" />

{{Blockquote|text=Yang took [[Hermann Weyl|[Hermann] Weyl]]'s place as the leading bird among my generation of physicists&nbsp;... With non-Abelian gauge fields generating nontrivial Lie algebras, the possible forms of interaction between fields become unique, so that symmetry dictates interaction. This idea is Yang's greatest contribution to physics. It is a contribution of a bird flying high over the rain forest of little problems in which most of us spend our lives.}}

=== 13 seminal contributions ===
In 2012, there were celebrations for Yang's 90th birthday. The [[Chinese University of Hong Kong]] hosted a scientific conference and dinner banquet to announce the creation of the CN Yang archive.<ref>{{Cite web |title=90th Birthday of Prof. C.N. Yang |url=https://www.iso.cuhk.edu.hk/english/publications/newsletter/article.aspx?articleid=54548 |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=香港中文大學資訊處 Information Service Office, CUHK |language=en-US |archive-date=December 6, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241206130513/https://www.iso.cuhk.edu.hk/english/publications/newsletter/article.aspx?articleid=54548 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Celebrations in Honour of Prof. C.N. Yang's 90th Birthday |url=https://www.iso.cuhk.edu.hk/english/publications/newsletter/article.aspx?articleid=54644 |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=香港中文大學資訊處 Information Service Office, CUHK |language=en-US |archive-date=November 13, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241113160458/https://www.iso.cuhk.edu.hk/english/publications/newsletter/article.aspx?articleid=54644 |url-status=live }}</ref> Physicist [[Kenneth Young (physicist)|Kenneth Young]] opened the ceremony.<ref name=":5" /> Yang also received a black cube from Tsinghua University<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Zhai |first=Hui |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QwGVEAAAQBAJ&dq=Chen-Ping+Yang+bethe&pg=PA580 |title=Festschrift In Honor Of The C N Yang Centenary, A: Scientific Papers |date=August 3, 2022 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-12-6416-0 |language=en |chapter=Pioneering a Field Forty Years Prior to its Birth}}</ref> with 13 of his seminal contributions engraved on the faces of the cube. On the cube is also written "Congratulations on Professor Chen Ning Yang's 90th birthday" in Chinese. The cube also includes an ancient Chinese poem used by Yang in his 2013 ''Selected Papers and Commentaries''; it reads:<ref name=":4" />

{{Poem quote
|A piece of literature
Is meant for the millennium
But its ups and downs are known
Already in the author's heart
|sign=[[Du Fu]]}}

The 13 contributions engraved on the cube are:<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Shi |first=Yu |date=July 10, 2014 |title=Beauty and physics: 13 important contributions of Chen Ning Yang |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0217751X14750013 |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics A |volume=29 |issue=17 |pages=1475001 |doi=10.1142/S0217751X14750013 |arxiv=1702.01901 |bibcode=2014IJMPA..2975001S |issn=0217-751X}}</ref>

* Statistical mechanics:
** [[Phase transition]]s (1952): for his works with Lee on the [[Lee–Yang theory]] and the [[Lee–Yang theorem]], which describe the liquid-gas phase transition based on microscopic properties.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Brink |first1=Lars |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4F22DAAAQBAJ&dq=Lee%E2%80%93Yang+circle+theorem,&pg=PA178 |title=60 Years Of Yang-mills Gauge Field Theories: C N Yang's Contributions To Physics |last2=Phua |first2=Kok Khoo |date=April 21, 2016 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4725-57-6 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" />
** [[Boson]]s (1957): for [[Lee–Huang–Yang correction]] for a [[weakly interacting Bose gas]], in collaboration with Lee and [[Kerson Huang]]. It explains the stability of [[Bose–Einstein condensate]]s and [[Superfluidity|superfluids]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Stoof |first1=Henk T. C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-9c2Ns2J5P4C&dq=Lee%E2%80%93Huang%E2%80%93Yang+corrections&pg=PA251 |title=Ultracold Quantum Fields |last2=Dickerscheid |first2=Dennis B. M. |last3=Gubbels |first3=Koos |date=November 30, 2008 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4020-8763-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6" />
** [[Yang–Baxter equation]] (1967): consistent condition for a one-dimensional factorized scattering many-body system, which resurrected the interest in the [[Bethe ansatz]] and allowed to better description of 1D fermions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=McCoy |first=Barry M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P2MVDAAAQBAJ&dq=yang+baxter+equations+history&pg=PA408 |title=Advanced Statistical Mechanics |date=2010 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-955663-2 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" />
** Finite temperature (1969): for the Yang–Yang thermodynamics formalism for 1D bosons, in collaboration with his brother [[Chen-Ping Yang]] (1930–2018<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chen Ping Yang {{!}} Department of Physics |url=https://physics.osu.edu/people/yaang.0 |access-date=October 22, 2025 |website=physics.osu.edu |language=en |archive-date=March 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240308002101/https://physics.osu.edu/people/yaang.0 |url-status=live }}</ref>).<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Bethe Ansatz: Yang-Yang formalism; Gibbs free energy |url=https://integrability.org/e_l_YY.html |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=integrability.org |archive-date=November 11, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241111144625/https://integrability.org/e_l_YY.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":4" /> The predictions of this formalism where demonstrated in 2008 using [[ultracold atom]]s.<ref name=":6" />
* Condensed matter physics:
** [[Magnetic flux quantum|Flux quantization]] (1961): for [[Byers–Yang theorem]] in [[Superconductivity|superconductors]], in collaboration with [[Nina Byers]]. They showed that the magnetic flux trapped in a superconducting ring is given by half of the usual [[magnetic flux quantum]].<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Byers |first1=N. |last2=Yang |first2=C. N. |date=July 15, 1961 |title=Theoretical Considerations Concerning Quantized Magnetic Flux in Superconducting Cylinders |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.46 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=46–49 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.46 |bibcode=1961PhRvL...7...46B |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
** [[off-diagonal long-range order|ODLRO]] (1962): for his development of the concept of [[off-diagonal long-range order]] (ODLRO) that characterizes [[macroscopic quantum phenomena]] like superconductivity and superfluidity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=C. N. |date=October 1, 1962 |title=Concept of Off-Diagonal Long-Range Order and the Quantum Phases of Liquid He and of Superconductors |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.34.694 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=694–704 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.34.694 |bibcode=1962RvMP...34..694Y |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":4" />
* Particle physics:
** Parity non-conservation (1956): for predicting the violation of [[Parity (physics)|parity]] symmetry with Lee, for which they were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957.<ref name=":4" />
** [[CPT symmetry|T, C, and P]] (1957): work on explaining the relation between parity (P), [[C-symmetry|charge]] (C) and [[T-symmetry|time-reversal]] (T) symmetries, now known as [[CPT symmetry]]. Done in collaboration with Lee and [[Reinhard Oehme]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=T. D. |last2=Oehme |first2=Reinhard |last3=Yang |first3=C. N. |date=April 15, 1957 |title=Remarks on Possible Noninvariance under Time Reversal and Charge Conjugation |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.106.340 |journal=Physical Review |volume=106 |issue=2 |pages=340–345 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.106.340 |bibcode=1957PhRv..106..340L |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
** Neutrino experiment (1960):  for the Lee and Yang paper that proposed to study the weak interaction with high energy neutrinos. This work promoted various neutrino experiments.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=T. D. |last2=Yang |first2=C. N. |date=March 15, 1960 |title=Theoretical Discussions on Possible High-Energy Neutrino Experiments |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.4.307 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=307–311 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.4.307 |bibcode=1960PhRvL...4..307L |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
** CP nonconservation (1964): for his paper on [[CP violation]], in collaboration with T. T. Wu.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Tai Tsun |last2=Yang |first2=C. N. |date=September 21, 1964 |title=<nowiki>Phenomenological Analysis of Violation of $\mathrm{CP}$ Invariance in Decay of ${K}^{0}$ and ${\overline{K}}^{0}$</nowiki> |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.380 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=13 |issue=12 |pages=380–385 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.380 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":4" />
* Field theory:
** Gauge theory (1954): for [[Yang–Mills theory]], in collaboration with [[Robert Mills (physicist)|Robert Mills]].<ref name=":4" />
** Integral formalism (1974): for giving meaning to the nonintegral phase factor in gauge theories.<ref name=":4" />
** Fiber bundle (1975): for the  [[Wu–Yang dictionary]], in collaboration with T. T. Wu.<ref name=":4" />
{{clear|right}}

=== Awards and places named after him ===
Yang was the first president of the Association of Asia Pacific Physical Societies (AAPPS) when it was established in 1989.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AAPPS |url=https://aapps.org/content/historicalBackgroundView.do |access-date=March 26, 2024 |website=www.aapps.org |language=ko |archive-date=March 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240326152759/https://aapps.org/content/historicalBackgroundView.do |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1997, the AAPPS created the C. N. Yang Award in his honor to highlight young researchers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AAPPS: C.N. Yang Award |url=https://aapps.org/content/awardView.do |access-date=March 26, 2024 |website=www.aapps.org |language=ko |archive-date=March 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240326152800/https://aapps.org/content/awardView.do |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1998, after his retirement, the Institute of Theoretical Physics of [[Stony Brook University]] was renamed [[C. N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Van Nieuwenhuizen |first=Peter |chapter=Frank Yang at Stony Brook and the Beginning of Supergravity |date=2022 |title=Dialogues between Physics and Mathematics: C. N. Yang at 100 |pages=1–17 |editor-last=Ge |editor-first=Mo-Lin |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-17523-7_1 |access-date=October 21, 2025 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-17523-7_1 |isbn=978-3-031-17523-7 |editor2-last=He |editor2-first=Yang-Hui|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> The C. N. Yang Hall, a residence hall and activity center at Stony Brook University, was dedicated in 2010.<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 23, 2010 |title=C.N. Yang Hall Dedication Ceremony |url=https://news.stonybrook.edu/homespotlight/c-n-yang-hall-dedication-ceremony-2/ |access-date=November 27, 2022 |publisher=Stony Brook University |archive-date=November 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221127023909/https://news.stonybrook.edu/homespotlight/c-n-yang-hall-dedication-ceremony-2/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
